title: Chemical Thermodynamics
subject: Chemistry
subtitle: Class 12 HSC & MHT-CET • Rapid Revision Deck

cards.q: Types of Thermodynamic Systems and Boundaries?
cards.a:
1. Open System: Can exchange BOTH energy and matter with its surroundings (e.g. Hot water in an open beaker, living organisms).
2. Closed System: Can exchange ENERGY (heat/work) but NOT matter with surroundings (e.g. Water in a sealed metallic flask).
3. Isolated System: Can exchange NEITHER energy nor matter with surroundings; perfectly insulated and sealed (e.g. Hot tea in an ideal vacuum thermos flask, the Universe).
cards.hint: The Universe is considered the ultimate isolated system.

cards.q: Extensive Properties vs Intensive Properties with examples?
cards.a:
1. Extensive Properties: Depend directly on the quantity / amount of matter present in the system.
- Examples: Mass ($m$), Volume ($V$), Internal Energy ($U$), Enthalpy ($H$), Entropy ($S$), Gibbs Free Energy ($G$), Heat Capacity ($C$).
2. Intensive Properties: Independent of the quantity of matter present; depend only on nature and concentration.
- Examples: Temperature ($T$), Pressure ($P$), Density ($\rho$), Melting point, Boiling point, Refractive index, Surface tension, Viscosity, Specific heat capacity ($c$).
cards.hint: The ratio of two extensive properties is always an INTENSIVE property (e.g. Density = Mass / Volume; Molarity = Moles / Volume).

cards.q: State Functions vs Path Functions and Thermodynamic Processes?
cards.a:
1. State Functions: Depend ONLY on initial and final states of system, independent of the path followed ($P, V, T, U, H, S, G$).
2. Path Functions: Depend on the path followed to achieve the change (Heat $q$, Work $w$).
Thermodynamic Processes:
- Isothermal: $T = \text{constant} \Rightarrow \Delta T = 0$ (for ideal gas, $\Delta U = 0, \Delta H = 0$).
- Adiabatic: $q = 0$ (no heat exchange with surroundings; insulated container).
- Isobaric: $P = \text{constant} \Rightarrow \Delta P = 0$.
- Isochoric: $V = \text{constant} \Rightarrow \Delta V = 0 \Rightarrow w = -P\Delta V = 0$.
- Cyclic: Initial state = Final state $\Rightarrow \Delta U = 0, \Delta H = 0, \Delta S = 0$.
cards.hint: Heat ($q$) and Work ($w$) are NOT state functions; they are path functions.

cards.q: Reversible vs Irreversible Thermodynamic Processes?
cards.a:
1. Reversible Process:
- Driving force is infinitesimally greater than opposing force ($P_{ext} = P \pm dP$).
- Takes place in infinite number of infinitesimal steps; system remains in virtual equilibrium at all stages.
- Yields MAXIMUM WORK ($W_{\text{max}}$); purely theoretical/ideal.
2. Irreversible Process:
- Driving force is substantially greater than opposing force ($P_{ext} \ll P$ or finite difference).
- Takes place in a single or finite rapid steps; equilibrium established only at end.
- Yields less than maximum work; all natural spontaneous processes are irreversible.
cards.hint: Maximum work is obtained ONLY when the process is conducted reversibly.

cards.q: IUPAC Sign Conventions for Heat (q) and Work (w)?
cards.a:
IUPAC Rules:
- Heat absorbed by the system from surroundings = $+q$ (endothermic)
- Heat released by the system to surroundings = $-q$ (exothermic)
- Work done ON the system (compression) = $+w$
- Work done BY the system (expansion) = $-w$
Formula for Pressure-Volume ($PV$) work against constant external pressure:
$w = -P_{\text{ext}} \Delta V = -P_{\text{ext}} (V_2 - V_1)$.
- Expansion ($V_2 > V_1$): $w$ is NEGATIVE (work done by system).
- Compression ($V_2 < V_1$): $w$ is POSITIVE (work done on system).
cards.hint: In free expansion against vacuum ($P_{\text{ext}} = 0$): $w = -0 \times \Delta V = 0$ (no work is done!).

cards.q: Maximum Work ($W_{\text{max}}$) in Isothermal Reversible Expansion of an Ideal Gas?
cards.a:
Expression:
$W_{\text{max}} = -2.303 n R T \log_{10} \left( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right)$
In terms of pressure (since by Boyle's law $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2 \Rightarrow V_2/V_1 = P_1/P_2$):
$W_{\text{max}} = -2.303 n R T \log_{10} \left( \frac{P_1}{P_2} \right)$
Where:
- $n$ = number of moles of ideal gas
- $R$ = $8.314\text{ J}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}$
- $T$ = absolute temperature in Kelvin.
cards.hint: In compression ($V_2 < V_1$ or $P_2 > P_1$), minimum work required to compress gas reversibly has the same magnitude but positive sign.

cards.q: First Law of Thermodynamics: Mathematical formulation and special cases?
cards.a:
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed from one form to another.
Mathematical Formulation:
$\Delta U = q + w$
Special Cases:
1. Isothermal process (ideal gas, $\Delta U = 0$): $q = -w$ (heat absorbed equals work done by system).
2. Isochoric process (constant volume, $\Delta V = 0 \Rightarrow w = 0$): $\Delta U = q_v$ (heat absorbed equals change in internal energy).
3. Adiabatic process ($q = 0$): $\Delta U = w_{\text{ad}}$ (work done on system increases internal energy).
4. Isobaric process: $q_p = \Delta U + P\Delta V = \Delta H$.
cards.hint: $q_v = \Delta U$ (heat at constant volume); $q_p = \Delta H$ (heat at constant pressure).

cards.q: Enthalpy (H): Definition and relationship between $\Delta H$ and $\Delta U$?
cards.a:
Enthalpy ($H$): Total heat content of a system at constant pressure:
$H = U + P V$
For finite change at constant pressure:
$\Delta H = \Delta U + P\Delta V$
For chemical reactions involving gases (substituting $P\Delta V = \Delta n_g R T$):
$\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g R T$
Where $\Delta n_g = \sum n_{g(\text{products})} - \sum n_{g(\text{reactants})}$.
Relationships:
1. If $\Delta n_g = 0 \Rightarrow \Delta H = \Delta U$ (e.g. $H_{2(g)} + I_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2 HI_{(g)}$)
2. If $\Delta n_g > 0 \Rightarrow \Delta H > \Delta U$ (e.g. $PCl_{5(g)} \rightarrow PCl_{3(g)} + Cl_{2(g)}$)
3. If $\Delta n_g < 0 \Rightarrow \Delta H < \Delta U$ (e.g. $N_{2(g)} + 3 H_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2 NH_{3(g)}$).
cards.hint: Calculate $\Delta n_g$ ONLY for gaseous species; ignore solid and liquid species completely!

cards.q: Hess's Law of Constant Heat Summation: Statement and application?
cards.a:
Statement: Enthalpy change ($\Delta H$) of a chemical reaction is the same whether the reaction takes place in a single step or in a series of steps.
- Because enthalpy ($H$) is a STATE FUNCTION, path does not affect overall $\Delta H$.
Application:
1. Calculating enthalpies of reactions that cannot be measured directly in a calorimeter (e.g. $C_{(\text{graphite})} + \frac{1}{2}O_{2(g)} \rightarrow CO_{(g)}$).
2. Calculating lattice enthalpy of ionic crystals via Born-Haber cycle.
3. Calculating bond enthalpies.
cards.hint: If a reaction equation is multiplied by factor n, multiply $\Delta H$ by n; if reversed, change the sign of $\Delta H$.

cards.q: Standard Enthalpy of Formation ($\Delta_f H^\circ$) and Reaction Enthalpy from $\Delta_f H^\circ$?
cards.a:
Standard Enthalpy of Formation ($\Delta_f H^\circ$): Enthalpy change accompanying the formation of 1 mole of a compound from its constituent elements in their standard reference states (at 298.15 K and 1 bar).
- By convention, $\Delta_f H^\circ$ of pure elements in standard states = 0 (e.g. $O_{2(g)}, N_{2(g)}, C_{(\text{graphite})}, Fe_{(s)}, Br_{2(l)} = 0$).
Reaction Enthalpy Formula:
$\Delta_r H^\circ = \sum \Delta_f H^\circ (\text{products}) - \sum \Delta_f H^\circ (\text{reactants})$.
cards.hint: For Carbon, $\Delta_f H^\circ(\text{graphite}) = 0$, but $\Delta_f H^\circ(\text{diamond}) = 1.89\text{ kJ/mol}$ (diamond is not standard reference state).

cards.q: Bond Enthalpy and calculation of Reaction Enthalpy from Bond Enthalpies?
cards.a:
Bond Enthalpy: Average energy required to break 1 mole of a specific covalent bond in gaseous molecules into isolated gaseous atoms.
Formula for Reaction Enthalpy:
$\Delta_r H^\circ = \sum \Delta H_{\text{bond}}(\text{Reactants broken}) - \sum \Delta H_{\text{bond}}(\text{Products formed})$
Note the reverse order:
- From $\Delta_f H^\circ$: $\text{Products} - \text{Reactants}$
- From Bond Enthalpies: $\text{Reactants} - \text{Products}$ (Bonds broken is endothermic +, bonds made is exothermic -).
cards.hint: Bond breaking is always ENDOTHERMIC ($+ \Delta H$); bond making is always EXOTHERMIC ($- \Delta H$).

cards.q: Entropy (S): Concept, definition, units, and Second Law of Thermodynamics?
cards.a:
Entropy ($S$): Thermodynamic state function measuring the degree of randomness, molecular disorder, or chaos in a system.
Mathematical definition:
$\Delta S = \frac{q_{\text{rev}}}{T}$
Units: $J\cdot K^{-1}$ or $J\cdot K^{-1}\cdot mol^{-1}$.
Second Law of Thermodynamics:
In any spontaneous / natural process, the total entropy of the universe (system + surroundings) always INCREASES:
$\Delta S_{\text{total}} = \Delta S_{\text{sys}} + \Delta S_{\text{surr}} > 0$.
- At equilibrium: $\Delta S_{\text{total}} = 0$
- Non-spontaneous process: $\Delta S_{\text{total}} < 0$.
cards.hint: Entropy order: Gas $\gg$ Liquid $>$ Solid.

cards.q: Entropy changes in Phase Transitions (Fusion, Vaporization, Sublimation)?
cards.a:
At phase transition equilibrium temperature:
1. Entropy of Fusion:
$\Delta_{\text{fus}} S = \frac{\Delta_{\text{fus}} H}{T_f}$
(where $T_f$ is melting/freezing point in Kelvin).
2. Entropy of Vaporization:
$\Delta_{\text{vap}} S = \frac{\Delta_{\text{vap}} H}{T_b}$
(where $T_b$ is boiling point in Kelvin; Trouton's rule: $\Delta_{\text{vap}}S \approx 88\text{ J}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}$ for most liquids).
3. Entropy of Sublimation:
$\Delta_{\text{sub}} S = \frac{\Delta_{\text{sub}} H}{T_{\text{sub}}}$.
cards.hint: All phase changes from solid $\rightarrow$ liquid $\rightarrow$ gas have POSITIVE $\Delta S$ (disorder increases).

cards.q: Gibbs Free Energy (G): Gibbs-Helmholtz equation and Spontaneity criteria?
cards.a:
Gibbs Energy ($G$): The maximum portion of energy of a system that can be converted into useful non-expansion work at constant T and P:
$G = H - T S$
Gibbs-Helmholtz Equation at constant T and P:
$\Delta G = \Delta H - T \Delta S$
Spontaneity Criteria at constant T and P:
1. If $\Delta G < 0$ (negative): Process is SPONTANEOUS (exergonic).
2. If $\Delta G = 0$: System is at EQUILIBRIUM.
3. If $\Delta G > 0$ (positive): Process is NON-SPONTANEOUS in forward direction (endergonic).
cards.hint: $\Delta G$ is the ultimate single master criterion for spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure.

cards.q: Effect of Temperature on Reaction Spontaneity (The 4 Case Table)?
cards.a:
From $\Delta G = \Delta H - T \Delta S$:
1. $\Delta H = (-)$ and $\Delta S = (+)$ $\Rightarrow \Delta G$ is ALWAYS NEGATIVE $\rightarrow$ Spontaneous at ALL temperatures.
2. $\Delta H = (+)$ and $\Delta S = (-)$ $\Rightarrow \Delta G$ is ALWAYS POSITIVE $\rightarrow$ Non-spontaneous at ALL temperatures.
3. $\Delta H = (-)$ and $\Delta S = (-)$ $\Rightarrow \Delta G$ is negative ONLY at LOW temperature ($T < \Delta H / \Delta S$) $\rightarrow$ Spontaneous at low T.
4. $\Delta H = (+)$ and $\Delta S = (+)$ $\Rightarrow \Delta G$ is negative ONLY at HIGH temperature ($T > \Delta H / \Delta S$) $\rightarrow$ Spontaneous at high T.
cards.hint: Equilibrium temperature at which process switches from non-spontaneous to spontaneous: $T_{\text{eq}} = \Delta H / \Delta S$ (where $\Delta G = 0$).

cards.q: Relationship between Standard Gibbs Energy ($\Delta G^\circ$) and Equilibrium Constant (K)?
cards.a:
Equation:
$\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + 2.303 R T \log_{10} Q$
At equilibrium, $\Delta G = 0$ and reaction quotient $Q = K$:
$\Delta G^\circ = -2.303 R T \log_{10} K = -R T \ln K$
Inferences:
1. If $K > 1 \Rightarrow \log K > 0 \Rightarrow \Delta G^\circ < 0$ (products favored at equilibrium).
2. If $K = 1 \Rightarrow \log K = 0 \Rightarrow \Delta G^\circ = 0$.
3. If $K < 1 \Rightarrow \log K < 0 \Rightarrow \Delta G^\circ > 0$ (reactants favored at equilibrium).
cards.hint: A large negative $\Delta G^\circ$ corresponds to a huge equilibrium constant $K$, driving reaction to near completion.

cards.q: Third Law of Thermodynamics and Absolute Entropies?
cards.a:
Statement (Nernst, 1906):
At absolute zero temperature ($T = 0\text{ K}$ or $-273.15^\circ\text{C}$), the entropy of a perfectly crystalline substance is strictly ZERO ($S = 0$).
Significance:
- Allows calculation of absolute entropy ($S^\circ$) of any pure chemical substance at any temperature $T$:
$S_T = \int_0^T \frac{C_p}{T} dT$
- Glassy/amorphous solids and crystals with molecular disorder (e.g. CO, $N_2O$, ice) have residual entropy $> 0$ even at 0 K.
cards.hint: Third law does not apply to amorphous substances because they retain residual entropy at 0 K.

cards.q: Work done in a chemical reaction: Formula $w = -\Delta n_g R T$?
cards.a:
For a reaction carried out at constant temperature and pressure:
Work done by gas: $w = -P_{\text{ext}} \Delta V = -\Delta n_g R T$
Where $\Delta n_g = n_{g(\text{products})} - n_{g(\text{reactants})}$.
Example: Oxidation of carbon monoxide:
$2 CO_{(g)} + O_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2 CO_{2(g)}$
$\Delta n_g = 2 - (2 + 1) = 2 - 3 = -1$
$w = -(-1) R T = +R T$ (work is done ON the system, compression).
cards.hint: If $\Delta n_g < 0$, work is positive (compression); if $\Delta n_g > 0$, work is negative (expansion).

cards.q: Enthalpy of Atomization ($\Delta_{\text{a}} H^\circ$) and Enthalpy of Ionization ($\Delta_{\text{ion}} H^\circ$)?
cards.a:
1. Enthalpy of Atomization ($\Delta_{\text{a}} H^\circ$): Enthalpy change accompanying the complete dissociation of 1 mole of a substance into isolated gaseous atoms (e.g. $CH_{4(g)} \rightarrow C_{(g)} + 4 H_{(g)}, \Delta_a H^\circ = 1665\text{ kJ/mol}$; average C-H bond enthalpy = $1665 / 4 = 416.25\text{ kJ/mol}$).
2. Enthalpy of Ionization ($\Delta_{\text{ion}} H^\circ$): Enthalpy change when 1 mole of a weak electrolyte completely ionizes in aqueous solution.
cards.hint: For a diatomic gas like $H_2$, enthalpy of atomization is identical to its bond dissociation enthalpy.

cards.q: Enthalpy of Solution ($\Delta_{\text{sol}} H^\circ$) and Lattice Enthalpy ($\Delta_L H^\circ$)?
cards.a:
Dissolution of an ionic solid $MX_{(s)}$ in water occurs in two steps:
1. Dissociation into gaseous ions (Lattice Enthalpy, $\Delta_L H^\circ$, endothermic):
$MX_{(s)} \rightarrow M^+_{(g)} + X^-_{(g)}$ ($\Delta_L H^\circ > 0$)
2. Hydration of gaseous ions by water (Hydration Enthalpy, $\Delta_{\text{hyd}} H^\circ$, exothermic):
$M^+_{(g)} + X^-_{(g)} + \text{aq} \rightarrow M^+_{(\text{aq})} + X^-_{(\text{aq})}$ ($\Delta_{\text{hyd}} H^\circ < 0$)
Total Enthalpy of Solution:
$\Delta_{\text{sol}} H^\circ = \Delta_L H^\circ + \Delta_{\text{hyd}} H^\circ$
- Substance dissolves easily if $|\Delta_{\text{hyd}} H^\circ| > \Delta_L H^\circ$.
cards.hint: Lattice enthalpy is always positive; hydration enthalpy is always negative.

cards.q: Calculation of Molar Heat Capacities: $C_p - C_v = R$ for an Ideal Gas?
cards.a:
Heat capacity $C = q / \Delta T$:
- At constant volume: $C_v = \left( \frac{\partial U}{\partial T} \right)_v$
- At constant pressure: $C_p = \left( \frac{\partial H}{\partial T} \right)_p$
Since $H = U + P V = U + R T$ (for 1 mole ideal gas):
$\Delta H = \Delta U + R \Delta T$
Dividing by $\Delta T$:
$C_p = C_v + R \Rightarrow C_p - C_v = R$
Molar heat capacity ratio $\gamma = C_p / C_v$:
- Monatomic gas: $\gamma = 5/3 \approx 1.67$
- Diatomic gas: $\gamma = 7/5 = 1.40$
- Triatomic/Polyatomic nonlinear: $\gamma = 4/3 \approx 1.33$.
cards.hint: $C_p$ is always greater than $C_v$ because gas does work of expansion at constant pressure.

cards.q: Why is melting of ice at 25°C spontaneous even though it is endothermic?
cards.a:
Melting of ice: $H_2O_{(s)} \rightarrow H_2O_{(l)}$
- $\Delta H > 0$ (endothermic, heat absorbed to break ice lattice)
- $\Delta S > 0$ (liquid water has much greater disorder than crystalline ice)
From $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$:
At 25°C (298 K), the temperature $T$ is high enough such that the favorable entropy term $T\Delta S$ EXCEEDS $\Delta H$ ($T\Delta S > \Delta H$):
$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S < 0$ (negative, spontaneous!).
cards.hint: Melting of ice is an ENTROPY-DRIVEN spontaneous process.

cards.q: MHT-CET Calculation: Calculate $\Delta U$ when 2 moles of an ideal gas expand into vacuum.
cards.a:
Free expansion against vacuum ($P_{\text{ext}} = 0$):
$w = -P_{\text{ext}} \Delta V = -0 \times \Delta V = 0$
If the process is isothermal (constant temperature):
For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature $\Rightarrow \Delta U = 0$.
From first law: $q = \Delta U - w = 0 - 0 = 0$.
All three quantities are ZERO: $w = 0, q = 0, \Delta U = 0$.
cards.hint: In free expansion of ideal gas into vacuum: $w = 0, q = 0$, and $\Delta U = 0$.

cards.q: Enthalpy of Neutralization: Strong Acid vs Strong Base vs Weak Acid?
cards.a:
Enthalpy change when 1 equivalent of acid is completely neutralized by 1 equivalent of base in dilute aqueous solution:
- For Strong Acid + Strong Base: $\Delta_{\text{neut}} H^\circ = -57.1\text{ kJ/equiv} = -13.7\text{ kcal/equiv}$ (CONSTANT value because the net reaction is always $H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O$).
- For Weak Acid + Strong Base (e.g. $CH_3COOH + NaOH$): $\Delta_{\text{neut}} H^\circ = -55.8\text{ kJ/mol}$ (LESS negative because some heat is consumed in ionizing the weak acid).
- Enthalpy of ionization of $CH_3COOH = 57.1 - 55.8 = 1.3\text{ kJ/mol}$.
cards.hint: Heat of neutralization of strong acid by strong base is a constant -57.1 kJ/mol.

cards.q: MHT-CET Trap: Predict sign of $\Delta S$ for crystallization, boiling of egg, and stretching rubber band.
cards.a:
1. Crystallization of liquid into solid $\rightarrow \Delta S = (-)$ (order increases, liquid $\rightarrow$ solid lattice).
2. Boiling / Hardening of an Egg $\rightarrow \Delta S = (+)$ (denaturation of globular proteins unfolds coiled chains into disordered random coils!).
3. Stretching of a Rubber Band $\rightarrow \Delta S = (-)$ (uncoiled tangled polymer chains align in an orderly parallel fashion).
4. Dissolution of sugar in water $\rightarrow \Delta S = (+)$ (orderly crystal dissolves into random solution).
cards.hint: High-yield trap: Boiling of an egg INCREASES entropy ($\Delta S > 0$) due to protein denaturation!
